title: Detection of Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
shortTitle: Detection of Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: This strategy covers T1048.003, exfiltration over an unencrypted, non command and control protocol, where data leaves the network inside protocol traffic that is either cleartext or normally used for something other than covert movement, such as file transfer, mail, or domain name lookups. Detection depends on proxy and firewall logs, flow records with byte counts, domain name system query logging, and payload level inspection where it exists, examined for a source that sends far more than it receives to an unusual destination. The failure in practice is scale: plenty of business applications upload large files, so the detection has to separate one host moving a large volume to an approved partner from a host streaming data to a host it has never contacted before.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for large amounts of data leaving your network. It watches channels that are not scrambled and not the usual remote control path. File transfer, mail, and name lookup traffic are common hiding places. It focuses on how much leaves and where it goes.
beginner.whyItMatters: Data that leaves is usually data lost. Unencrypted channels are easy for an attacker to use because almost every network allows them. They are also easier for you to monitor than scrambled channels. Spotting the transfer while it is running lets you cut the connection.
howItWorks: Firewalls and proxies log each connection with the bytes sent and the bytes received.
The detection calculates the ratio of outbound to inbound data for each host and each session.
It also groups sessions by destination and records whether that destination is new.
Domain name lookups for long random looking names are added as a second signal.
A host sending far more than normal to a new destination raises an alert with the volume shown.
beginner.example: Consider a building where everyone signs guests in at the front desk. One visitor arrives with an empty suitcase and leaves with it full. Nothing about the visit looks illegal, but the change in weight is worth a question. Counting bytes out compared with bytes in is the same simple check.
takeaways: Watch the size and direction of data, not only the protocol.
A new destination plus a large upload is the strongest combination.
Cleartext channels are your best chance to confirm what left.

objectives: Explain why unencrypted and non command channels are attractive for data theft
Use byte counts and direction ratios to identify bulk outbound transfers
Include name resolution patterns as supporting evidence
Correlate a transfer with the process and user that generated it
Distinguish approved business uploads from suspicious ones
Choose a severity that reflects the sensitivity of the data at risk
dataSources: Web proxy logs recording request method, destination, uploaded bytes, and user agent for each session
Firewall or network flow records with source and destination addresses, ports, and bytes transferred in each direction
Domain name system query logs including queried name, record type, response size, and requesting host
Mail relay logs showing outbound message size, attachment count, and recipient domains
Endpoint sensor records tying outbound sessions to a process image and the account that started it
logic: The detection scores outbound data volume against what the sending host normally does and against the destination's history in your environment. The fields that must be correlated are the source host and account, the process image initiating the transfer, the destination address and port, the outbound to inbound byte ratio, the total volume in the session, and whether that destination has ever been contacted before by any host. The benign case is a signed backup or file sharing client uploading to a partner address that many hosts already use, and the malicious case is a host uploading a large volume to a destination unique to that host, often alongside unusual name lookups or connections from a process that normally does not talk to the internet.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Large Outbound Transfer To First Seen Destination
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     BytesOut|gt: 50000000
#     DestinationFirstSeen: 'true'
#   filter:
#     DestinationCategory|contains: 'backup'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: Business users uploading large design or video files to an approved cloud storage provider
Backup or replication software sending a full backup to a new remote site for the first time
Application teams pushing container images or release artefacts to a registry outside the usual list
Research or analytics teams transferring datasets to a partner address that is new to the proxy
tuningNotes: Build a destination allow list from the top upload destinations per asset group, then alert only on destinations that are new or rare, and raise the volume threshold to sit above the normal ninety-ninth percentile for that group. Filter categories for approved backup, storage, and code hosting services, and scope the rule to servers holding regulated data rather than every workstation. Then add the process and account as tie breakers, so a known data tool from a known team is suppressed while an unknown binary uploads a large file. The coverage you lose is exfiltration to a well known cloud service that you allowed, so retain payload inspection or upload logging for those services where you can.
